task: Finalize this conceptual guide for application engineers choosing how to read a catalog during concurrent updates.
source_facts: All product names, behavior, identifiers, and examples in this fixture are synthetic. Hearth Catalog stores a catalog as numbered immutable generations. A commit publishes a complete new generation atomically. The current pointer identifies the most recently published generation. A read without a generation parameter resolves the current pointer when that individual request begins. Separate unpinned requests can therefore observe different generations if publication occurs between them. A pin selects one existing generation for subsequent reads; a pin does not block commits or freeze the current pointer. A pin belongs to exactly one catalog. Pin lifetime is 30 minutes from creation. Reading through a pin does not extend its lifetime. A request that begins while its pin is valid can complete after expiration. A new request using an expired pin returns HTTP 410. A pinned read never silently falls back to the current generation. A paginated listing carries its pin identity in every continuation token, so pages in that listing share a generation. If the pin expires before the next page request begins, that next request returns HTTP 410. A client needing a complete consistent listing must then create a new pin and restart the listing from its first page; it must not append the restarted listing to already collected pages. Stable exports are a use case for pins. A dashboard whose tiles can tolerate different generations can use unpinned reads. Publication is independent of readers. In the worked example, generation 41 is current at 09:00, an export creates a pin for generation 41 at 09:01, and a commit publishes generation 42 at 09:03. A dashboard request beginning at 09:04 without a pin observes generation 42, while the export using its valid pin continues to observe generation 41. These times illustrate ordering rather than a publication schedule. A pin is a read-consistency mechanism rather than a write lock. No stronger cross-request consistency guarantee applies to unpinned reads.

# Reading a catalog while it changes

## Summary

Hearth Catalog separates publication from read consistency. Each commit publishes an immutable generation, and readers can either follow the current generation or pin an existing one. Use a pin when several requests must describe the same catalog state. Use unpinned reads when each request can independently observe the latest published state.

This distinction matters for work that spans requests. A single successful read does not establish which generation a later unpinned read will use. Conversely, a long-running pinned export does not stop another writer from publishing an update.

## Generations and the current pointer

A generation is a numbered, immutable version of one catalog. A commit publishes a complete new generation atomically. The current pointer identifies the most recently published generation; it does not turn an older generation into a mutable object.

An unpinned request resolves the current pointer when that request begins. If publication occurs between two requests, the first can read the earlier generation and the second can read the later one. Both requests can succeed while describing different catalog states. There is no stronger consistency promise connecting those separate unpinned reads.

## What a pin establishes

A pin selects one existing generation for subsequent reads. Each pin belongs to exactly one catalog. It gives a sequence of requests a stable read target, but it does not block commits or freeze the current pointer. Think of the pin as a consistency choice for a reader, rather than a write lock held against publishers.

A pin lasts 30 minutes from creation. Reading through it does not extend that lifetime. This fixed lifetime matters when an export performs many requests: continued activity is not evidence that the pin remains valid.

Expiration is evaluated when a request begins. A request that begins with a valid pin may finish after the pin expires. A new request using an expired pin returns HTTP 410. A pinned read never silently switches to the current generation.

## A publication seen by two readers

The following sequence illustrates ordering, not a scheduled publication interval:

| Time | Event | Read consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 09:00 | Generation 41 is current | New unpinned reads select 41. |
| 09:01 | An export pins generation 41 | Its subsequent pinned reads select 41. |
| 09:03 | A commit publishes generation 42 | The current pointer now identifies 42. |
| 09:04 | A dashboard starts an unpinned request | The dashboard selects 42. |

At 09:04, the export can still read generation 41 through its valid pin. The dashboard and export see different generations because they chose different consistency modes, not because publication was partial.

## Pagination and expiration

A paginated listing includes its pin identity in every continuation token. While that pin remains valid, the pages describe the same generation. The token carries the listing's consistency context; it does not renew the pin.

If the pin expires before a later page request begins, that request returns HTTP 410. To obtain a complete consistent listing, create a new pin and restart from the first page. Do not append the restarted listing to pages already collected under the expired pin, because the new pin may select a different generation.

## Choosing a read mode

A stable export needs pages that describe one catalog state, so it uses a pin and handles expiration as a restart boundary. A dashboard whose tiles tolerate different generations can use unpinned reads. In either case, publishers remain free to commit: the reader's choice determines visibility across requests, not whether publication can proceed.
